Article Title: Landslide hits Sikkim’s Mangan, partially blocks Teesta River flow
Article Text:
Landslide occurred above the Chyakoong River, opposite OC Bhir, during the intervening night of September 5 and 6.

Sikkim, September 6: A landslide occurred above the Chyakoong River in Sikkim’s Mangan district during the intervening night of September 5 and 6, authorities said.The district administration received reports from the district police and Chungthang Sub-Division police about the incident near OC Bhir. A large section of the hillside along a newly constructed road cutting of the Naga-Tosa Road in the Naga Forest area collapsed near the confluence of the Teesta and Chyakoong rivers, opposite the Theng Tunnel.According to the ANI report, the landslide partially blocked the flow of both rivers, temporarily obstructing the Teesta and raising concerns about further disruption to water flow in the area.The Teesta River is currently flowing normally, although water has accumulated in both the Teesta and Chyakoong rivers. Water continues to flow through both rivers despite the accumulation.The Station House Officer of Chungthang CP/PS and personnel at Theng CP are monitoring the situation on the ground.Water levels at Sankalang OP and Phidang OP remain normal, although the river water has turned muddy. Authorities at both locations have been instructed to closely monitor water levels and report any significant changes immediately, according to an official release.The Police Control Room has also been alerted and directed to warn vulnerable areas in the lower belt as a precaution.
Article Summary: A landslide occurred above the Chyakoong River in Sikkim’s Mangan district during the intervening night of September 5 and 6. A large section of the hillside along a newly constructed road cutting of the Naga-Tosa Road collapsed near the confluence of the Teesta and ChYakoong rivers, opposite the Theng Tunnel. The Teesta River is currently flowing normally, although water has accumulated in both rivers. Water continues to flow through both rivers despite the accumulation.

NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Sunday shared a video of his interaction with three students who were injured during police action amid recent student protests in Bihar.The three were part of a group of students from Bihar who met the Lok Sabha leader of opposition at his Delhi residence on September 3. In a social media post, Gandhi said the three students had been “shot at”, referring to a protest in Siwan, Bihar, on July 25.“Think about it: what crime had these children committed that they were shot? They had asked the government for just three things — education, employment, and accountability,” the Raebareli MP wrote on X.The leg bone of one of the students, he added, was shattered after he was hit by a bullet fired from an AK-47.“Along with it, his dream of joining the Army and serving the country was shattered too. Bullets tore through the shoulders of two other students,” Rahul Gandhi wrote.“They were not criminals. They were children from poor families who had gone out to study carrying the dreams of their families — some wanted a good job, while others wanted to change the circumstances of their homes,” he added.The Congress leader further remarked that while their physical wounds would heal, there is no answer to how the psychological trauma they had suffered could be treated."Mr prime minister, Mr chief minister — their broken bones will heal. Can you give them back their broken dreams?" Rahul Gandhi said, questioning Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Bihar chief minister Samrat Choudhary.Several parts of Bihar witnessed student protests, some of which turned violent, on July 25 as part of a broader agitation by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) in Delhi. The CJP was leading protests demanding the resignation of then-Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET paper leak issue, along with reforms in the education system.The CJP, which had been protesting at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar since June 21, called off its agitation on July 25, shortly after Pradhan resigned. Union minister Pralhad Joshi has since been given additional charge of the Education ministry.The Bihar government has told the Supreme Court that a police constable fired four rounds from an AK-47 into the air after being trapped in a crowd, while maintaining that no protester was injured in the firing. The constable has since been suspended.

NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Sunday said India had voted in favour of a United Nations General Assembly resolution promoting the use of equal-area world map projections. It also made it clear that the measure does not endorse any particular map and that India’s sovereign territory must be depicted according to its official map.The MEA said the resolution neither adopts nor authenticates any particular world map and does not address political cartography, including international boundaries, disputed territories or place names.India nevertheless used its explanation of vote to reiterate its position on Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.“India’s sovereign territory, including the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, must be depicted in accordance with India’s official map. Any inaccurate or misleading depiction is unacceptable. Our position on India’s sovereignty and territorial integrity is clear, consistent and non-negotiable.”The UN General Assembly adopted the resolution, titled “Correct the Map: Rebalancing Global Cartographic Representation and Promoting Equitable Representation of the World’s Regions, Particularly Africa”, on September 4 by a vote of 164 to one.The resolution encourages the use of equal-area projections that preserve the relative sizes of continental landmasses. However, India clarified that it should not be interpreted as endorsing any specific map, projection or depiction of national boundaries.“We believe that the resolution should be understood as supporting the broader use and consideration of equal-area map projections and not as endorsing the Equal Earth projection or any other specific map projection,” Indian diplomat Raghoo Puri said while explaining India’s vote.
Article Summary: The UN General Assembly adopted the resolution, titled “Correct the Map: Rebalancing Global Cartographic Representation and Promoting Equitable Representation of the World’s Regions, Particularly Africa’, on September 4 by a vote of 164 to one. The resolution encourages the use of equal-area projections that preserve the relative sizes of continental landmasses.

Article Title: What's cooking? A kitchen fix to cut dementia risk in old age
Article Text:
Cooking is a complex task from neurological point of view: Doc

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

New Delhi: What if one of the simplest ways to keep the brain active later in life is already sitting in the kitchen? A six-year study from Japan has found that older adults who cooked at home at least once a week were less likely to develop dementia requiring long-term care than those who cooked less often.The population-based study followed 10,978 adults aged 65 years and older and recorded 1,195 cases of dementia during the six-year follow-up. After accounting for demographic, socioeconomic and health-related factors, men who cooked at least once a week had a 23% lower risk of dementia, while women had a 27% lower risk, compared with those who cooked less than once a week. The association was even stronger among people with low cooking skills. Among them, more frequent home cooking was associated with a 67% lower risk of dementia in older adults.The findings, published in the Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health, were based on data from the Japan Gerontological Evaluation Study. Researchers assessed cooking frequency and skills at the beginning of the study and then tracked dementia requiring care through Japan's public long-term care insurance records.Dr (Col) Joy Dev Mukherji, chairman and head, neurology, Max Super Speciality Hospital, Saket, said cooking is a surprisingly complex activity from a neurological point of view. "It involves planning, attention, working memory, while also combining movement and sensory stimulation," he said. However, he cautioned against interpreting the findings as proof that cooking prevents dementia.“This was an observational study and does not prove that cooking prevents dementia. It is also possible that people in the early stages of cognitive decline may gradually stop cooking because of difficulties with planning and memory,” he said.Dr Manjari Tripathi, head of neurology at AIIMS, highlighted the social dimension of cooking, saying preparing meals with friends, family or the wider community could provide additional cognitive and social engagement. She also encouraged men to cook, saying the activity must not be viewed as restricted to women.Interestingly, the association was strongest among people with lower cooking skills, possibly because less experienced cooks engage more in planning and problem-solving. However, this was not established by the study. Doctors said the broader message is to remain engaged in meaningful activities involving learning, planning, movement and social interaction, rather than viewing cooking as a treatment for dementia.
Article Summary: Six-year study from Japan found older adults who cooked at home at least once a week were less likely to develop dementia requiring long-term care. The association was even stronger among people with low cooking skills. More frequent home cooking was associated with a 67% lower risk of dementia in older adults.

NEW DELHI: Coal stocks at thermal power plants across the country have fallen to less than half the recommended level, with 50 plants classified as having 'critically low' inventories as on Sept 2 amid high electricity demand and monsoon-led disruptions in supplies, Central Electricity Authority data showed.The plants, with a combined capacity of around 224 GW, had 28.2 million tonnes (MT) of coal as of Wednesday, 48% of the prescribed requirement of 58.7 MT. The available stock is equivalent to about nine days of coal requirement at 85% plant load factor, against the normal requirement of around 19 days.The plants classified as short on coal stocks have less than 25% of their normative inventories. Coal ministry officials, however, said all critical plants were being monitored by an inter-ministerial team of officials on a day-to-day basis and regular fuel supplies were being provided to them.Of the 50 plants, 45 are based on domestic fuel, four are designed for imported coal and one runs on washery rejects.A senior coal ministry official said, "Classification of a thermal power plant as critical is a routine monitoring parameter under norms laid down by CEA. It simply means closer tracking and priority action. These plants are not running out of supply."Though the normative coal requirement at power plants is calculated at 3.1 MT every day at 85% plant load factor, officials said the actual requirement is around 2.4 MT.The monsoon sees supply disruptions every year. The situation starts improving from Sept onwards as rains begin to recede.While the power ministry did not respond to requests for a reaction, sources said some coal-fired plants had been asked to defer scheduled maintenance to ensure continuity of electricity generation.
Article Summary: Coal stocks at thermal power plants across the country have fallen to less than half the recommended level. 50 plants classified as having 'critically low' inventories as on Sept 2. High electricity demand and monsoon-led disruptions in supplies blamed.

NEW DELHI: Authorities on Saturday demolished a mosque located inside the district magistrate's office complex in Uttar Pradesh's Saharanpur after a court upheld an earlier order declaring the structure illegal.Senior administrative officials, including the district magistrate and sub-divisional magistrate, reached the site as bulldozers began demolishing the structure. The collectorate complex was placed under heavy security, with Provincial Armed Constabulary (PAC) personnel deployed and all gates shut as a precaution.Meanwhile, Samajawadi Party MP Iqra Hussain claimed that she was put under house arrest at her residence ahead of her scheduled visit to Saharanpur.Hasan said that a large police force was deployed outside her residence overnight and prevented her from leaving for Saharanpur."A large police force was deployed at my Kairana residence overnight, and I was placed under house arrest to prevent me from going to Saharanpur. I intended to visit Saharanpur to meet officials regarding the Collectorate mosque issue and to voice the concerns of the people of my constituency, but I was not even allowed to leave my home," Hasan told news agency ANI."In a democracy, public representatives are elected to raise the voice of the people. That voice cannot be suppressed by stopping me," she added.The demolition came a day after the district judge's court dismissed an appeal filed by the Muslim side challenging the City Magistrate's order.On September 4, the district judge's court, after hearing arguments from both sides and examining the evidence presented, upheld the city magistrate's order declaring the mosque illegal.The city magistrate's court had on July 17 ordered the demolition of the mosque and imposed compensation of around Rs 6.41 crore on the occupants over alleged illegal encroachment and misuse of government land.The case was initiated following a complaint by Vikas Tyagi, former provincial coordinator of Bajrang Dal, who alleged that the mosque had been built illegally inside the DM office complex, a sensitive government premises where confidential administrative work is carried out.The complaint also alleged that the premises were being used for commercial purposes apart from religious activities. According to the allegations, a post office was operating from the site and some rooms had been rented out to outsiders, with the mosque committee allegedly collecting monthly rent.The district administration had argued that the alleged encroachment and commercial use of the premises raised security concerns, particularly given the sensitive nature of government operations conducted there.The development comes amid similar administrative action against alleged illegal religious structures in various parts of Uttar Pradesh.

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan criticised police officers over the alleged assault on protesting students during the NEET agitation at Jantar Mantar and said that the detachment expected of officials appears to be disappearing.While speaking at the launch of former secretary (security) Yashovardhan Azad's book "Policing the Republic", Justice Bhuyan said that police must maintain their credibility because people seek their help when they feel wronged."All of us are dismayed when we see young officers of the Indian Police Service personally going and assaulting protesters and demonstrators. This is something very, very distressing to observe. The detachment expected of police officers somehow seems to be disappearing, and this is indeed a matter of grave concern," Justice Bhuyan said."For most common people, a policeman on the street wearing a whistle and a lathi represents the power and authority of the state. When they feel wronged, they seek the help of the police. It is, therefore, of utmost importance that the police force maintains its credibility.It can do so only by strictly adhering to the Constitution, by functioning as a truly professional force, acting impartially, displaying courage and acting with conviction, maintaining integrity and adhering to secular principles, thereby upholding the rule of law," he said.The Supreme Court judge further said that if government functionaries become lawbreakers, it is bound to breed contempt for the law and encourage lawlessness."If the functionaries of the government become lawbreakers, it is bound to breed contempt for the law and will encourage lawlessness. No civilised nation can permit that to happen. Does a citizen shed his fundamental right the moment a policeman arrests him?" Justice Bhuyan said.The alleged use of force by Delhi Police during the July 20 student protests at Jantar Mantar and the march towards Parliament has come under the Supreme Court's scrutiny, with the court constituting a high-level panel to examine complaints of excessive force.The panel, headed by former Supreme Court judge Justice R Subhash Reddy, will investigate allegations against Delhi Police and examine evidence including CCTV footage and videos of the protests.Among the allegations to be examined are the use of lathis, tear gas, pellet guns and electronic batons, as well as claims of targeted harassment and molestation of women protesters.
Article Summary: Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan criticised police officers over the alleged assault on protesting students during the NEET agitation. NEW DELHI: Jalandhar Commissionerate Police detained Manjit Singh Bedi, a fugitive wanted in the US in connection with an alleged SNAP benefits fraud case, Punjab Director General of Police Gaurav Yadav said on Friday.Bedi was reportedly placed on the US Most-Wanted Fraudsters list over allegations of defrauding the US government of more than $600,000 through a scheme involving Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits. According to the Punjab DGP, Bedi allegedly fled to India via Canada in April 2026 to evade US law enforcement."In a major breakthrough, Jalandhar Commissionerate Police apprehends Manjit Singh Bedi, a wanted fugitive linked to a US-based benefits fraud case. Bedi was reportedly placed on the US Most-Wanted Fraudsters list in connection with a SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) benefits fraud case in the #USA and had allegedly fled to #India via #Canada in April 2026 to evade the law," the DGP posted on X.The FBI had earlier alleged that Bedi, an India-born naturalised US citizen, operated Asian Grocery Store in Tacoma, Washington, where he used customers' Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) cards to process transactions without providing food.He allegedly gave SNAP participants cash instead and kept half of the proceeds.“Instead of selling participants food, Bedi is alleged to have swiped their cards and given them cash,” the FBI said in its wanted notice.Bedi was indicted in the US on charges of wire fraud and SNAP benefits fraud. He was initially allowed to appear in court without being arrested and was ordered to surrender his passport and remain in Washington state, but the FBI said he later fled to Canada and then India.A federal arrest warrant was issued against him on May 21, 2026, in the US District Court for the Western District of Washington after he allegedly violated the conditions of his supervision. The FBI had offered a reward of up to $150,000 for information leading to his arrest and conviction.The Punjab DGP said the police force remains committed to tracking fugitives and tackling transnational organised crime.“Punjab Police remains relentless in tracking down fugitives and dismantling transnational organised crime networks, ensuring that no one can evade justice by crossing borders,” he said.In a separate development earlier on Friday, the State Special Operation Cell (SSOC) Amritsar and Counter Intelligence Amritsar arrested six people in two operations targeting alleged weapons and narcotics smuggling modules.Police recovered 2.9 kg of heroin, eight high-end pistols and six live cartridges, besides impounding a car and a motorcycle allegedly used in the smuggling activities.Preliminary investigation indicated that the accused were allegedly involved in cross-border smuggling and received weapons and narcotics consignments through drones for distribution among criminal elements in Punjab, the DGP said. Further investigation is underway to establish the network's forward and backward linkages.

Article Title: SC awards pension to Mumbai engineer who forged ST certificate
Article Text:
SC allowed him to superannuate in peace with retirement benefits

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court has rewarded a wrongdoer - a man who got appointed as a junior civil engineer in Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai (MCGM) by producing a forged ST certificate, and, subsequently, stalled the scrutiny of his eligibility for quota for more than a decade - by allowing him to superannuate in peace with retirement benefits.Shirish P Patil got a certificate in 1984 by identifying himself as belonging to the 'Tokre Koli' Scheduled Tribe community. Based on the certificate, he was appointed a junior civil engineer in MCGM in 1994. He misplaced the original ST certificate but managed to secure a fresh one from the sub-divisional magistrate, Bhusawal division, in Oct 2000.Following scrutiny initiated by MCGM, the Police Vigilance Cell traced Patil's family history and found that his ancestors had been recorded as 'Koli', 'Hindu Koli' and 'Hindu Suryawanshi Koli', none of which belonged to the ST category. In July 2009, MCGM issued a show cause notice to Patil.He successfully dodged and delayed proceedings before the scrutiny committee until Jan 2020, when the panel rejected his plea that his lawyer and elderly family members were not available, and invalidated the ST certificate. HC dismissed his appeal against cancellation of ST status.SC, however, stayed Patil's dismissal from service through an interim order on Nov 18, 2021.As a result, the engineer continued to serve until June 30, 2025, when he retired after being employed with MCGM for more than three decades based on a forged ST certificate.A bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi Thursday upheld the cancellation of Patil's ST certificate and Bombay HC order. However, it took a lenient view given his undertaking that he or any of his family members "shall (not) be entitled to claim any future benefit on the basis of the invalidated ST certificate".The ruling contrasts with SC's consistent rulings against benefits accruing to people who forge SC or ST certificates to gain admission or employment.
Article Summary: Shirish P Patil got a certificate in 1984 by identifying himself as belonging to the 'Tokre Koli' Scheduled Tribe community. Based on the certificate, he was appointed a junior civil engineer in MCGM in 1994. In July 2009, MCGM issued a show cause notice to Patil. He successfully dodged and delayed proceedings before the scrutiny committee.

Article Title: 'Cracked skull' wasn't all: In eye of storm, 'influencer' Swatantra Bhardwaj
Article Text:
Swatantra Bhardwaj, 22, was detained in Uttar Pradesh's Bulandshahr district.

A provocative online presence

The hunt for Bhardwaj

(With inputs from PTI)

Poll Vote & Share your view Is the government doing enough to hold influencers accountable for their actions online? Yes, they are taking action No, they need to do more 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion





NEW DELHI: Long before the viral video in which he boasted about assaulting a Jantar Mantar protester’s father, 'influencer' Swatantra Bhardwaj had built a sizeable following through provocative posts, political associations and incendiary remarks.Bhardwaj, 22, was detained in Uttar Pradesh's Bulandshahr district on Friday, hours after Delhi Police assured protesters from the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) that he would be arrested within 72 hours.Bhardwaj is accused of assaulting the father of student activist Nishu Azad during a protest at Jantar Mantar in Delhi on July 20.His detention came after a clip from an interview went viral in which Bhardwaj is heard claiming that he had "cracked the skull" of the father."Do you know which section this crime attracts? Section 307. He needed 60 stitches. The man was being taken away in an ambulance in serious condition. His daughter was standing outside the police station and saying that she would die by suicide if her father didn't get justice."But I was not even jailed. The world should know this. I was out and about through the night," Bhardwaj is heard saying in the video.He then named several political leaders while explaining why, according to him, he had little reason to fear arrest."I have the blessings of Hanuman upon me. And secondly, Kapil Mishra is my elder brother. They say Kapil Mishra called and I was released. Chirag Paswan is my elder brother. How many leaders do you know? Do you know Modi ji? Modi ji is also my elder brother. I have everyone's support," he claimed.There is, however, no evidence to establish that any of the political leaders named by Bhardwaj intervened on his behalf in the case.The viral clip also brought renewed attention to Bhardwaj's older social media posts and videos.According to news agency PTI, his Facebook page, which has around 327,000 followers, contains posts focused on cow protection, attacks on Muslims and critics of the government, as well as photographs appearing to show his proximity to political figures and official events.Some older videos circulating on social media purportedly show him making inflammatory remarks about Muslims and government critics. In others, he boasts about his political connections and claims he does not fear arrest.His online presence suggests that the persona seen in the viral clip was not an isolated episode, but part of a broader public image he had cultivated over time.On Thursday, a day before his detention, Bhardwaj shared a screenshot showing his name among the trends on X, captioning it, "Love you all Virodhi".He also posted a photograph on Instagram showing a 'kada' on his wrist with the caption "Feel the power!". The post appeared to reference a Delhi Police statement that Kumar had been injured by a 'kada' and "not by any weapon".His social media accounts also featured photographs with political leaders, including Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary, Delhi minister Kapil Mishra and Union minister Chirag Paswan.Paswan said on Friday that Bhardwaj had misused his name and the names of other leaders.The Union minister for food processing industries said he had lodged a complaint against Bhardwaj and demanded action against him."No action despite the accused admitting to an attack that could have been fatal sets a bad example; I take responsibility for ensuring justice for the family," Paswan said.Bhardwaj's accounts also included what appeared to be AI-generated images of him with women wearing burqas or hijabs.One particularly violent image, posted on 22 May, showed Bhardwaj holding the bloodied chin of a man. The accompanying text referred to "Mughal" and included the words "aa gaya swad".His Instagram account, which had around 184,000 followers, was deactivated on Friday. He also has a verified account on X with more than 6,400 followers.The viral video intensified demands for action against Bhardwaj, with protesters raising the issue during the CJP demonstration in Delhi on Friday.Police subsequently deployed several teams to trace him.According to police officials, Bhardwaj had travelled to Bulandshahr and was staying in Naithla village. He allegedly fled the village on a motorcycle towards Khurja before a police team could apprehend him.He was wearing a helmet, apparently in an attempt to conceal his identity, police said.Local residents told TOI that Bhardwaj had arrived in Bulandshahr early on Friday, allegedly to evade arrest, and had taken shelter at the home of a local family.While there, he interacted with some journalists and reportedly repeated his claims about the alleged assault during the CJP protest.Bhardwaj was staying at the house of Harishankar Sharma, a Naithla resident who works as a cab driver in the Delhi-NCR region.Sharma said he had met Bhardwaj during an earlier journey.“Bhardwaj called me and said he wanted to come to my house to meet me. He arrived early in the morning along with another man. Initially, I did not suspect anything. But when media persons started arriving at my village, I sensed something was wrong,” Sharma said.Sharma said Bhardwaj later asked to borrow his motorcycle, saying he would return “within five minutes”.“Then I came to know that Delhi Police had detained him. It was only after that I learnt that he was wanted in a criminal case in the national capital. I still do not know much about the case,” Sharma said.The detention came after CJP representatives said Delhi Police had assured them that Bhardwaj “will be arrested within 72 hours”.The case has since drawn attention not only to the alleged assault but also to the online persona Bhardwaj had built through provocative posts, political associations and claims of influence.
Article Summary: Swatantra Bhardwaj, 22, was detained in Uttar Pradesh's Bulandshahr district on Friday. He is accused of assaulting the father of student activist Nishu Azad during a protest at Jantar Mantar in Delhi on July 20. His detention came after a clip from an interview went viral in which he claimed he had "cracked the skull" of the father.

Article Title: Amazon techie leaves Rs 46 lakh package to join Indian Army, set to be commissioned at OTA Gaya
Article Text:
Shardendu Tiwari





LUCKNOW: Lucknow’s 27-year-old Shardendu Tiwari, who worked as a cloud engineer at Amazon with an annual package of around Rs 46 lakh, is set to be commissioned into the Army at the Officers Training Academy (OTA), Gaya, on Saturday.A second-generation soldier, Shardendu chose military service after leaving behind a corporate career and an opportunity with global aerospace company Airbus. His commissioning will mark the culmination of his journey from the technology sector to the armed forces.Shardendu resides in Neelmatha, Lucknow, and his family traces its roots to Pipergaon in Sultanpur district. His father, Honorary Captain Raj Kumar Tiwari, served in the Army Service Corps for 36 years before retiring. Inspired by his father, Shardendu developed an inclination towards joining the armed forces during his childhood.He completed his schooling at Kendriya Vidyalaya, Chandimandir, Haryana. He pursued a Bachelor of Engineering degree in Information Technology and later completed an MTech in Computer Science and Information Security from Punjab Engineering College, Chandigarh.Shardendu appeared for Army selection eight times before succeeding.He joined through the technical entry route, which enabled him to serve in the Army while remaining connected with technology.“I was also drawn to the armed forces because of the opportunities they offer for adventure and field service,” he said.During training at OTA Gaya, his leadership qualities earned him the appointment of Senior Under Officer (SUO), one of the highest cadet appointments at the academy. He enjoys playing basketball and table tennis.
Article Summary: Shardendu Tiwari, 27, is set to be commissioned into the Army at the Officers Training Academy (OTA), Gaya, on Saturday. His commissioning will mark the culmination of his journey from the technology sector to the armed forces. Shardendu chose military service after leaving behind a corporate career and opportunity with global aerospace company Airbus.

Article Title: With bare hands, lone warrior cleans up dumpyard of a river
Article Text:
21-year-old BSc student has been a solitary warrior against civic mess and pollution in his hometown

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

BHOPAL: His online followers know him as 'Bittu Tabahi'. In reality, Surendra Singh Choudhary is the exact opposite of what the moniker 'Tabahi', meaning destruction, implies.For the past seven months, this 21-year-old BSc student has been a solitary warrior against civic mess and pollution in his hometown, Biaora in MP's Rajgarh district, picking up plastic bottles, tangled weeds and other solid waste from Ajnar river, which had virtually become a dumpyard.With no heavy machinery or protective gear at his disposal, he removed the garbage with his bare hands, often at great risk to his health.Bittu's dogged pursuit has helped restore a section of the river, earning him widespread praise across the country and an invite from CM Mohan Yadav Saturday. They had a warm exchange at the CM's residence in Bhopal, where Yadav assured Bittu of every possible support from govt.The chief minister also shared a video on X, calling Bittu a "son of Biaora" who not only restored Ajnala (the river stretch passing through Biaora) to its original form through sheer resolve and effort, but also sent out a larger message that one man's determination is all it takes to bring meaningful change.There were also reports that the CEO of an organisation from the Netherlands had offered him a job, but Bittu said he had only heard this from media reports. "I am yet to receive any information about it first hand," he told TOI.Encouraged by his success, Bittu, whose parents work in the health department, has decided to expand his work. "My sole objective is to keep my hometown clean. I have decided to take my work to other public places," he said.Bittu started his mission on Republic Day this year. Upset that everyone complained about the mess, but none - including the municipal administration - addressed it, the college-goer decided to get his hands dirty. From removing garbage piles on streets to pulling out weeds from water bodies, his activism eventually drew national attention.Unfortunately, his selfless service is being undone by the same people he is trying to help. In his interaction with the chief minister, Bittu shared the pain of watching people throw garbage into the river again, oblivious to the effort that went into cleaning it. "I don't know why people keep dumping waste into the river," he said, his voice betraying anger.The silver lining is that the local municipal corporation has now woken up to its civic mandate, and has deployed JCBs and Poclain machines to clear waste piles from the streets. However, the larger problem - habitual littering and a lack of collective ownership - remains unaddressed.
Article Summary: Surendra Singh Choudhary, 21, has been a solitary warrior against civic mess and pollution in his hometown, Biaora. With no heavy machinery or protective gear at his disposal, he removed the garbage with his bare hands. Bittu's dogged pursuit has helped restore a section of the river, earning him widespread praise across the country.

Article Title: Nepal floods show the risk; China's mega-dam raises bigger questions for India
Article Text:
Recent Nepal floods highlight Himalayan vulnerabilities and cascading disaster risks. China's Yarlung Tsangpo dam project faces scrutiny due to its geologically unstable location. The dam's operation could influence downstream river flows and water security for India. Chinese scientists have warned about the project's seismic and landslide risks in the region. India faces managing combined risks from infrastructure, climate change, and border proximity.

Why the Brahmaputra is so important

China began construction of the Yarlung Tsangpo River Lower Reaches Hydropower Project in July last year.

What did experts find

Is China capable of ‘stopping’ the Brahmaputra?

What India is concerned

What does Nepal’s recent disaster show?

How climate change is adding to the risk

The ecological concerns

Dam can affect Earth’s rotation

China calls Brahmaputra project safe

The problem of hydrological data

Why is transparency important?

A Himalayan warning for India

The rain came down relentlessly, turning quiet mountain streams into raging torrents and narrow roads into muddy rivers. Across Nepal, floodwaters and debris swept through homes, roads and hydropower facilities, leaving behind broken bridges, stranded communities and villages cut off from the outside world.In the mountains, where steep slopes already make life precarious, swollen rivers, landslides and collapsing rock can quickly turn a natural hazard into a cascading disaster.For communities living along narrow Himalayan valleys, a sudden rush of water, ice and debris can leave little time to escape.The recent flash floods in Nepal have brought these vulnerabilities sharply into focus. Search teams have battled heavy rain and thick layers of debris while looking for people believed to be trapped in tunnels, hydropower projects and underground power facilities along the Bhotekoshi River.But the devastation has also raised a larger question: what happens when the already fragile Himalayan environment is combined with increasingly large infrastructure projects, including dams, tunnels, highways and hydropower facilities?That question has particular significance for India because the Himalayas are not confined by political boundaries. Rivers, glaciers, mountain systems and geological faults cut across China, Nepal, Bhutan and India.A disaster originating in the high mountains can therefore have consequences far beyond the point where it begins.It is against this backdrop that China's massive hydropower project on the Yarlung Tsangpo, known downstream as the Brahmaputra, has come under renewed scrutiny.The project, being built in Tibet's Medog County at the dramatic Great Bend of the river, is expected to become the world's largest hydropower project.Its location, however, adds another layer of concern. The project sits in one of the world’s most geologically challenging regions, marked by steep Himalayan terrain, active faults, earthquakes, landslides, glaciers and extreme weather.These natural risks make the dam not just a massive engineering undertaking, but also a strategically sensitive project located upstream of one of India’s most important rivers.China formally began construction of the Yarlung Tsangpo River Lower Reaches Hydropower Project in July last year. The mega-dam is being built in Medog County, near the river’s Great Bend, where the Yarlung Tsangpo makes a dramatic U-turn before entering India.China calls the Brahmaputra the Yarlung Tsangpo. After crossing into Arunachal Pradesh, the river is known as the Siang or Dihang before flowing through Assam and eventually entering Bangladesh, where it is known as the Jamuna.The project is located in one of the world’s deepest river gorges. Over a stretch of about 50 kilometres, the river drops nearly 2,000 metres, creating enormous potential for hydropower generation.The project is expected to comprise five cascade hydropower stations and generate more than 300 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity annually, more than three times the annual generation of China’s Three Gorges Dam, according to reports cited in the material.With an estimated cost of around 1.2 trillion yuan, or about $167.8 billion, it is set to rank among the world’s most expensive infrastructure projects. Chinese Premier Li Qiang has described it as the “project of the century”.But the significance of the project extends far beyond its size or power-generation capacity.The Brahmaputra is far more than a river. It is an economic, ecological and strategic lifeline for millions of people across the eastern Himalayas and South Asia.Originating on the Tibetan Plateau, the river flows through China, India and Bangladesh before emptying into the Bay of Bengal. It stretches for roughly 2,900 kilometres and drains a basin of about 580,000 square kilometres shared by China, India, Bhutan and Bangladesh.One of the world’s largest rivers by discharge, the Brahmaputra is also known for its vast braided channels. Its waters support agriculture, irrigation, fisheries, transport, hydropower and ecosystems across the region.For India, the river becomes particularly important after entering Arunachal Pradesh and Assam. The Brahmaputra and its tributaries sustain communities, farmland and ecosystems across the Northeast, while also bringing the region some of its most destructive floods.That is what makes China’s position upstream so significant for India. Beijing cannot simply stop the Brahmaputra from flowing into India. By the time the river reaches Arunachal Pradesh, it has already begun receiving substantial water from rainfall and tributaries, with flows rising sharply during the monsoon.The concern is therefore less about China being able to permanently cut off the river and more about whether a large upstream hydropower system could influence the timing and volume of flows.The operation of reservoirs, tunnels, power stations and other infrastructure could potentially affect seasonal water releases.For India, this raises questions not only about water security, but also about access to reliable hydrological information and the ability to prepare for sudden changes in river flows, particularly during periods of heavy rainfall or extreme weather.The study, published in the Chinese-language journal Sedimentary Geology and Tethyan Geology and supervised by the state-owned China Geological Survey, examined the Paizhen Fault in Tibet.According to the researchers, the fault has remained highly active since the Pleistocene epoch, or Ice Age, and continues to show evidence of geological activity. Geological dating of ancient lake sediments suggests that movement along the fault occurred as recently as about 9,500 years ago.The researchers warned that repeated movement along the fault had fractured and weakened surrounding rock formations. This could make major engineering structures in the area more vulnerable to geological hazards."The Paizhen area is located within the reservoir area of the Yarlung Tsangpo downstream hydropower station," the paper said.The researchers said the fault could have a significant impact on the structural stability and construction of nearby infrastructure, including dams, roads, bridges and tunnels, as well as the reservoir area.They also cited the magnitude 6.9 earthquake that struck the Milin area of Tibet in 2017 as evidence that the region remains seismically active."Under regional seismic action, landslides and collapses can easily be induced, threatening the safety of engineering facilities and personnel," they said.The scientists recommended reinforcing vulnerable slopes and installing retaining structures to reduce the risk of landslides and collapses during construction and after the project becomes operational.The research was conducted by scientists from the Chengdu University of Technology, the Civil-Military Integration Centre of the China Geological Survey, and the Middle Yarlung Zangbo River Natural Resources Observation and Research Station.The findings are significant because they come from Chinese researchers working within China's own geological and scientific institutions.They do not establish that the project is unsafe or that a disaster will occur. But they underline the difficulty of constructing and operating a mega-project in a region where geological instability is an inherent feature of the landscape.The idea that China could simply stop the Brahmaputra from reaching India is often overstated. Srijan Pal Singh, author, former Advisor for Policy and Technology to former President APJ Abdul Kalam, CEO of Homi Lab and founder of Kalam Centre, said the more realistic concern was China's ability to influence the timing of flows and the lack of transparency surrounding the management of the river."The real concern, therefore, is less about China cutting off the Brahmaputra and more about transparency, reliable data-sharing, and India's ability to anticipate and manage sudden changes in flow," Singh had earlier told TOI.He said that while a significant share of the Brahmaputra's annual flow is generated within India through monsoon rainfall and tributaries, the lean-season flow originating in Tibet remains strategically important.Singh also cautioned against viewing the project solely through the lens of water diversion. "Any large dam on an international river has both economic and strategic implications," he said.He added that control over upstream infrastructure could itself create strategic influence even without physically restricting the river."It is not necessary to stop the flow of water for leverage to exist. The ability to regulate flows, collect hydrological data, or alter the timing of water releases can shape the decisions of downstream countries, particularly during periods of tension or extreme weather," he said.The distinction matters because the principal challenge for India is not simply the quantity of water but the predictability of that water.During the monsoon, India needs accurate information about upstream river conditions to prepare for floods. During the dry season, information about river flows becomes equally important for agriculture, water management and ecosystems.India’s concerns over the Medog project go beyond water security. The Yarlung Tsangpo flows from Tibet into Arunachal Pradesh. A mega infrastructure project on the river, close to the disputed border, therefore has an inevitable strategic dimension.The biggest concern may ultimately be geological. The project lies in the eastern Himalayas, along the collision zone of the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates.The region is marked by active faults, steep slopes, fractured rock, earthquakes and frequent landslides, all of which pose challenges for a mega-dam and the infrastructure needed to support it.The 1950 Assam-Tibet earthquake, estimated at magnitude 8.7, remains a stark reminder of the region’s seismic potential. It caused widespread destruction across Tibet and Assam and killed thousands of people.The Chinese geological study has added to concerns over the site. Researchers found that repeated fault activity had weakened rock formations and recommended measures such as reinforcing vulnerable slopes and constructing retaining structures to reduce landslide risks.Writing in Project Syndicate, Brahma Chellaney, professor emeritus of strategic studies at the New Delhi-based Centre for Policy Research, said the warning from Chinese scientists was particularly significant.“The geologists conclude that the terrain has a 'loose structure and weak cohesion' and warn that fault movement or an earthquake could easily trigger large-scale instability, threatening both the reservoir and surrounding infrastructure,” Chellaney wrote.“Ironically, the latest evidence suggests that China's scientific establishment understands the dangers of building the unprecedented super-dam more clearly than its political leadership appears willing to acknowledge. Now that China’s own geologists have raised the alarm, Beijing must embrace transparency and accept transboundary responsibilities before a potential water bomb is fully assembled upstream,” Chellaney wrote on X.There are also concerns about the possibility of reservoir-triggered seismicity, in which the weight of water stored behind a large dam can affect pressure and stress along existing faults. China’s 2008 Wenchuan earthquake has often been cited in this debate.Scientists have differed over the extent of the Zipingpu reservoir’s role, but some studies have suggested that the reservoir may have contributed to triggering or advancing seismic activity.The concern, therefore, is not only whether an earthquake could damage the dam. A major earthquake could also trigger landslides, rockfalls and failures across the surrounding infrastructure.Singh said advances in engineering have significantly improved dam safety but cannot completely remove geological risks.“Modern engineering can design dams to withstand very strong earthquakes. Advanced materials, flexible structural designs and continuous monitoring systems have greatly improved dam safety. However, no engineer can completely eliminate geological risk,” he said.The region has also witnessed glacier collapses and landslides. Sayanangshu Modak, a researcher at the University of Arizona, cited the massive 2021 glacier collapse near the Great Bend, which temporarily blocked the river and sharply raised water levels, SCMP reported.Long-term safety, he added, would depend on continuous monitoring, regular assessments and the ability of the project to withstand not only earthquakes but also landslides, rockfalls and extreme weather events.The August 26 disaster in Nepal offers a stark example of how Himalayan hazards can interact. The evidence available so far points to a glacier-rock collapse and massive debris avalanche rather than a conventional monsoon flood.The collapse triggered an ice-rock avalanche that temporarily blocked the Bhotekoshi River, sending a huge volume of ice, rock, mud and water downstream and causing widespread destruction.The avalanche reportedly travelled at around 50 metres per second. Such events demonstrate the cascading nature of Himalayan disasters.A glacier collapse or earthquake can trigger a landslide; a landslide can block a river; and the sudden failure of that blockage can send a destructive surge of water and debris downstream.Infrastructure located along the river corridor, including roads, bridges, hydropower stations and settlements, can then become part of the disaster chain.The 2015 Nepal earthquake provided another warning. Research following the quake found that earthquake-triggered landslides were a major cause of damage to hydropower infrastructure and estimated that about a quarter of existing, constructed and planned Himalayan hydropower projects faced a high probability of moderate-to-severe earthquake damage.Climate change is adding another layer of uncertainty to an already fragile landscape. Glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya are losing ice, while permafrost degradation can destabilise high-altitude slopes. Glacial lakes are expanding in some areas, while changing rainfall patterns are increasing the risk of extreme precipitation.Nepal has thousands of glacial lakes, some of which can potentially produce catastrophic Glacial Lake Outburst Floods, or GLOFs.Climate change does not cause every landslide, avalanche or flood. But it can alter the conditions that make such events more likely and make their timing and scale harder to predict.That creates a particular challenge for hydropower development in the Himalayas.As Himanshu Thakkar, coordinator of the South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers and People, has argued, environmental, social and disaster-risk assessments need to account for the specific characteristics and historical hazards of individual valleys.The Medog project is being built in an exceptionally sensitive landscape. The Great Bend of the Yarlung Tsangpo is marked by steep slopes, glaciers, high rainfall, unstable rock formations and active tectonic structures.Geologist Fan Xiao has described the Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon as a rare biodiversity hotspot in a geologically unstable region.He has warned that multiple hydropower stations, high dams, reservoirs and extensive tunnels could increase landslide risks and cause long-term environmental damage.The impact of such a project is also unlikely to be limited to the dam itself. Roads, tunnels, bridges, transmission lines, worker settlements and other supporting infrastructure will be needed to build and operate the project.Each intervention can alter slopes, drainage patterns and river corridors, creating additional pressure on an already fragile ecosystem.The ecological consequences are particularly difficult to predict over decades, especially as climate change continues to reshape the Himalayan environment.The project’s location also raises questions about its strategic implications for India. The concern is not simply that the dam could alter river flows. The infrastructure required to build and operate such a massive project could itself have strategic value.“Such a large project requires roads, tunnels, bridges, power infrastructure and communication networks. These assets can improve access to remote border areas and support logistics in peacetime as well as during a crisis,” Singh said.He added that while the project alone would not alter the military balance along the Line of Actual Control, it could increase China’s long-term presence near the border and improve its understanding of the terrain and river system.“The strategic balance in the eastern sector will continue to depend primarily on military capability, border infrastructure, surveillance and operational readiness on both sides,” he said.Singh also noted that India has accelerated hydropower development downstream as part of its effort to strengthen water utilisation.Some analysts, however, see the project as giving Beijing additional diplomatic leverage because of its upstream position. Shanghai-based security analyst Ni Lexiong told SCMP that the dam could “effectively create geopolitical leverage vis-a-vis India diplomatically”.Others take a more cautious view. Liu Zongyi, a senior fellow at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, argued that concerns about China’s ability to manipulate river flows are overstated and that the project would not fundamentally change India-China relations.For India, therefore, the challenge is broader than the question of whether China can control the Brahmaputra.It is about managing the combined risks of upstream infrastructure, uncertain hydrological flows, seismic hazards, climate change and the project’s proximity to a sensitive border.Earth’s rotation is not perfectly constant. Natural forces such as earthquakes, the Moon’s gravitational pull, melting ice and the movement of water can subtly change how quickly the planet spins. Even human-made structures can have a measurable, though extremely tiny, effect.China’s Three Gorges Dam provides one striking example. When its vast reservoir is filled, the enormous volume of stored water redistributes mass on Earth. This increases the planet’s moment of inertia, causing it to rotate very slightly more slowly.Nasa scientist Dr Benjamin Fong Chao calculated that the full reservoir could lengthen the day by about 0.06 microseconds, or 60 billionths of a second, while shifting the position of the poles by roughly two centimetres, BBC reported.The change is far too small to have any noticeable effect on everyday life. But it demonstrates how moving billions of tonnes of water can produce a measurable change in the planet’s physical dynamics.Beijing has repeatedly sought to reassure downstream countries about the safety of the Medog project. An official statement issued in December 2024 said the project was safe and prioritised ecological protection."Through extensive geological explorations and technical advancements, a solid foundation has been laid for the science-based, secure, and high-quality development of the project," it said.Chinese officials have also maintained that the project follows the highest industry standards and would not negatively affect downstream countries.A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said China was highly responsible in developing cross-border rivers and had extensive experience in hydropower construction. Beijing has also said it would maintain communication with downstream countries and cooperate on disaster prevention and mitigation.The recent geological study does not necessarily contradict those assurances in the sense of proving that the dam is unsafe. But it does demonstrate that the geological challenges identified by outside observers are also being studied by Chinese scientists themselves.For India, one of the most important lessons from the past is the importance of reliable river-flow information. China suspended the sharing of hydrological information on the Brahmaputra and Sutlej during the 2017 flood season.In a written reply in the Rajya Sabha on February 8, 2018, the Ministry of External Affairs said China had not provided hydrological information on the Brahmaputra and Sutlej despite existing bilateral agreements. Beijing attributed the interruption to "technical reasons".The suspension occurred during the 73-day Doklam standoff between India and China, although Beijing maintained that the interruption was related to the upgrading of hydrological monitoring stations.China resumed Brahmaputra hydrological data sharing in May 2018. The original agreement on sharing hydrological information for the Brahmaputra was signed in 2002 and subsequently renewed.For India and Bangladesh, the challenge is therefore broader than whether China can control the Brahmaputra. It involves the combined risks of upstream infrastructure, seismic hazards, climate change, ecological damage and uncertainty over future water flows.The sheer scale of what China has called the “project of the century” has also increased calls for greater transparency about the dam’s design, geological assessments, reservoir operations and possible downstream impacts.International principles governing transboundary rivers generally require countries to exchange relevant information, avoid significant cross-border harm and consult on projects that could affect other states.Chellaney has argued that China’s limited disclosure about the project is particularly concerning given its potential consequences for downstream countries.Singh said India’s immediate priority should be stronger mechanisms for information-sharing.“India's first priority should be to strengthen institutional mechanisms for the regular exchange of hydrological data, especially during the monsoon season,” he said.Chellaney argued that the warnings raised by Chinese researchers should prompt greater international scrutiny.“When scientists working under a communist regime issue such warnings, the international community must pay attention,” he wrote.For India, the Medog project is therefore not just a question of water. It is a question of how to manage a combination of geological, environmental and strategic risks on a river that crosses national borders and supports millions of people downstream.The recent disaster in Nepal has shown how quickly the Himalayas can turn from a source of water and energy into a source of extraordinary danger.A glacier can collapse. Rock can fall into a river. A temporary blockage can form. The blockage can breach. A wall of water and debris can then travel through a narrow valley at enormous speed.When roads, bridges, tunnels, hydropower plants and settlements occupy that same valley, the consequences multiply. This is the central challenge facing Himalayan development.The issue is not whether Nepal, India or China should develop their mountain regions. Millions of people depend on infrastructure, electricity, connectivity and economic development.The question is whether that development is being planned according to the realities of a young, unstable and rapidly warming mountain system.For India, the question becomes even more consequential because the country's major rivers originate or flow through these mountains before reaching the plains.China's Yarlung Tsangpo project therefore represents more than a massive power-generation scheme. It raises questions about seismic safety, river-flow management, ecological change, data sharing and strategic influence.The Himalayas are already under pressure from climate change, earthquakes, landslides, glacier retreat and intense rainfall. Adding more infrastructure without accounting for cumulative risk could create new vulnerabilities even while addressing existing strategic concerns.The immediate cause of Nepal's August 26 disaster may have been a glacier-rock collapse. But the larger warning is unmistakable: the Himalayas are becoming an increasingly dangerous place to ignore geological and climatic limits.As Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah said in his September 2 address to the House of Representatives, "climate change is the world's shared responsibility, and that Nepal must forcefully campaign for climate justice and international financial compensation rather than simple post-disaster aid".He linked the recent catastrophic flash floods in Rasuwa to a warming climate and described the disaster as a warning for the wider Himalayan region and the world.That warning extends beyond Nepal.The Brahmaputra does not recognise borders. Neither do earthquakes, glaciers, landslides or extreme weather. As China moves ahead with the Medog mega-project and India expands its own hydropower infrastructure, the real test will be whether development can keep pace with the risks of a rapidly changing Himalayas.As construction of the Medog project advances, the questions will become increasingly difficult to avoid: Can the world's largest hydropower project remain safe in one of the world's most geologically active landscapes? Can downstream countries receive timely and reliable information about changes in river flows?And can infrastructure development in the Himalayas be pursued without turning natural hazards into human-made disasters?For now, there are no easy answers. But the floods in Nepal have made one thing clear. In the Himalayas, the consequences of getting the balance between development and nature wrong can travel far beyond the valley where the decision was made.
Article Summary: Recent Nepal floods highlight Himalayan vulnerabilities and cascading disaster risks. China's Yarlung Tsangpo dam project faces scrutiny due to its geologically unstable location. The dam's operation could influence downstream river flows and water security for India. India faces managing combined risks from infrastructure, climate change, and border proximity.

Article Title: Work-life balance vs job security: The workplace trade-off Gen Z is challenging
Article Text:
The salary still matters

Security feels increasingly fragile

How much sacrifice is acceptable?

The stereotype problem

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What does the survey indicate?

Young workers are entering a labour market shaped by layoffs, artificial intelligence, intense competition and constantly changing skill requirements. At the same time, they have grown increasingly vocal about boundaries, mental health and the value of time outside the office.As the generational composition of the workforce continues to evolve, organisations seem to face new challenges in designing effective employee engagement strategies. Shaped by rapid technological change and globalisation, millennials and Generation Z bring distinct work values, communication preferences and expectations around career growth, flexibility and the workplace.For Gen Z, the ideal job increasingly sounds like a carefully negotiated deal: pay me well, give me room to grow, let me have a life after work and, preferably, give me some control over how I get the work done.A survey of young workers reflects that tension. Job security emerged as an important consideration, but work-life balance carried an equally strong pull. The responses suggest a generation trying to answer a difficult question: how much career stability is worth sacrificing personal freedom for?The survey found that 95% of respondents rated job security at the higher end of the importance scale, with 57.1% giving it the highest rating.At the same time, 90.5% also gave work-life balance equal weight.That makes the dilemma rather clear. Gen Z wants security. It also wants breathing room.The idea of Gen Z choosing lifestyle over money tells only one part of the story. The responses from young workers point to a more complicated calculation.Financial independence and building a successful career were each selected by 76.2% of respondents as among their biggest reasons for working. Achieving a particular lifestyle followed at 61.9%, while gaining experience and skills came in at 57.1%.Money remains a major part of the equation. Neeshu Shukla, a working professional from Delhi, said, “Better pay is important. Money is the deal breaker,” followed by timely hikes and promotions.For Shukla, however, the workplace equation extends beyond the payslip. She wants a professional but empathetic environment and opportunities to learn and grow. She also places value on skills, experience, capabilities and willingness to learn as the basis for determining an employee’s value.The broader survey reflects a similar hierarchy. Personal growth was the most-selected career priority apart from money, at 85.7%. Work-life balance followed at 66.7%, while good workplace culture stood at 61.9%. Career progression and job security were selected by 47.6% and 42.9%, respectively.The anxiety around stability also has a very practical source. Competition and low salaries were the biggest source of career insecurity in the survey, selected by 76.2% of respondents. Layoffs followed at 52.4%, while lack of job opportunities and lack of career growth each stood at 47.6%. Economic uncertainty was another concern for 42.9% of respondents. AI and automation were cited by 38.1%.That anxiety shows up in how respondents view the very idea of a “secure job”. More than seven in 10 said such security exists only in certain industries. Just 19% considered a secure job realistic in the broader economy.A recent Emeritus report titled ‘India’s Gen Z Outlook 2026’ found a similar shift in how young Indians think about careers. The study found that 74% of Gen Z respondents prioritise work-life balance over formal leadership titles, while 65% believe a successful career does not require becoming an executive leader.That finding adds another layer to the workplace debate. The traditional image of career success often comes with a predictable sequence: climb the ladder, take on more responsibility, earn more money and eventually reach a senior title.Gen Z appears to be questioning how attractive that ladder remains.Ashwin Damera, co-founder and CEO of Emeritus, described the shift as an overhaul of the traditional career path, driven by rapidly changing skills and jobs.The survey becomes particularly interesting when the questions move from preferences to trade-offs.Asked whether they would stay in a job they disliked if it offered excellent job security and financial stability, 19% said probably yes. Another 33.3% remained unsure, while 42.9% said probably not.Over 42% of respondents said they would immediately leave a high-paying job that seriously affected their mental health or personal life. A further 19% said their decision would depend on their financial situation.For Kajal Singh, an HR professional working at a consultancy firm in Delhi, the workplace she wants comes down to “flexible work options, better work-life balance & a supportive environment.”Harshita, a working professional from Bhopal, takes the idea of flexibility further. In her ideal workplace, she wants “flexibility and respect for the opinions of Gen Zs,” along with room for employees to decide how they execute their work.The pattern is not confined to India. A separate Deloitte 2026 survey of Gen Zs and millennials found that 55% of Gen Zs and 52% of millennials are delaying major life decisions because of financial pressures. Only 25% of Gen Zs and 21% of millennials prefer rapid career progression through frequent promotions, while just 6% in both groups identify leadership as their primary career goal.At the same time, 74% of both Gen Zs and millennials use AI to some extent in their day-to-day work, with many viewing it as an opportunity to improve productivity and open new career paths — even as they feel they are adapting faster than their organisations.Taken together, the findings point to a generation caught between two competing demands: the need for financial security and the refusal to define success solely by the traditional career ladder.The generation also appears to be tired of having that negotiation interpreted as a lack of ambition.More than half of respondents said older generations completely misunderstand Gen Z’s attitude towards work, while another 42.9% said they misunderstand it somewhat.The most irritating stereotype was the idea that “Gen Z doesn't want to work”, selected by 81% of respondents. “Gen Z quits too easily” followed at 76.2%. Other commonly selected stereotypes included being lazy, expecting too much and having no loyalty.For employers, that makes the Gen Z workplace conversation less about choosing between stability and balance and more about whether the two can exist together. For young workers, the bigger challenge is figuring out which compromises build a career and which ones slowly consume the life that career was supposed to support.
Article Summary: A survey of young workers reflects that tension. Job security emerged as an important consideration, but work-life balance carried an equally strong pull. The responses suggest a generation trying to answer a difficult question: how much career stability is worth sacrificing personal freedom for?

Article Title: One teacher, ten students: India's foundational classrooms hit a new benchmark
Article Text:
UDISE+ 2025-26 numbers show a system that added capacity, tightened ratios, expanded infrastructure

More teachers, lower ratios

Retention tells a similar mixed story

Fewer single-teacher schools, better-equipped classrooms

Growth in teacher numbers has also changed how schools are staffed

Women now make up most of the teaching workforce

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Report also points to a shift in who is doing the teaching

Every year, a child who stays in school through Class 12 rather than dropping out at 14 usually has one adult to thank for it more than any policy document: a teacher who noticed, who followed up, who made the difference between a student staying enrolled and quietly disappearing from the rolls. The Unified District Information System for Education Plus (UDISE+) 2025-26 report, released this month by the Union Ministry of Education, is built around that basic unit of the school system. It tracks how many teachers India has, how they're distributed, and what that distribution means for millions of students. The numbers show a workforce that has grown steadily even as the system around it has become leaner and retained more students.India's teacher count rose from 94,83,294 in 2022-23 to 98,07,600 in 2023-24, then to 1,01,22,420 in 2024-25 and 1,02,73,020 in 2025-26, an increase of 8.3% over four years, crossing the one-crore mark along the way. That growth is most evident in the Pupil-Teacher Ratio (PTR), which measures how many students each teacher is responsible for. At the Foundational level, the PTR now stands at 10 students per teacher, down from 11 in 2022-23.Preparatory has moved to 12 from 14, Middle school to 17 from 18, and Secondary to 21 from 23. All four levels are now well within the 30:1 ratio recommended under the National Education Policy; a lower PTR generally means more attention per student and classrooms that are easier to manage. The improvement has been gradual rather than sudden: Preparatory PTR, for instance, moved from 14 to 13 to 13 before settling at 12, showing the kind of steady year-on-year correction that comes from sustained recruitment rather than a one-time push.Dropout and retention figures follow the same broad trend, though not evenly across every level. Preparatory dropout fell from 8.7% in 2022-23 to 3.7%, then 2.3%, and now 1.8% in 2025-26, a decline of nearly 7 percentage points in four years. Secondary dropout came down from 13.8% to 7.0% over the same period, nearly halving. Middle school is the exception: after falling steadily from 8.1% to 5.2% to 3.5% across three years, its dropout rate ticked up slightly this year, from 3.5% to 3.6%, the only level where the four-year trend reversed rather than held.Retention tells a similar mixed story. Secondary retention jumped from 47.2% to 51.9%, helped by more schools now offering secondary education, and Middle retention rose from 82.8% to 83.7%, continuing a climb from 75.8% in 2022-23. Foundational retention eased this year, from 98.9% to 98.5%, after three straight years of gains from 92.1% in 2022-23. Preparatory retention also slipped, from 92.4% to 91.1% — but unlike Foundational, its four-year path wasn't a steady climb: it fell to 85.4% in 2023-24 before recovering to 92.4% the year after, and now sits only marginally above where it started in 2022-23, at 90.9%.Enrolment and transition numbers add to the picture. Secondary GER rose from 68.5% to 71.7% this year; across the four-year period it actually dipped to 66.5% in 2023-24 before climbing back and past its 2022-23 level of 67.6%. Middle GER has stayed roughly flat for four years, moving between 89.5% and 90.3% and settling at 89.6% now. Transition rates — the share of students who move on to the next stage rather than leaving school altogether — improved at every checkpoint: Foundational-to-Preparatory transition rose to 99.2% from 98.6%, Preparatory-to-Middle to 93.8% from 92.2%, and Middle-to-Secondary to 88.3% from 86.6%, each figure now at its highest point across the four years tracked.The growth in teacher numbers has also changed how schools are staffed. Single-teacher schools, where one person handles every grade and subject, fell by about 3% in 2025-26 to 1,00,843, continuing a decline from 1,18,190 in 2022-23 and 1,10,971 the year after. Zero-enrolment schools fell even faster — by around 29% in a single year, from 7,993 to 5,663, though the number had actually risen to 12,954 in 2023-24 before the sharp correction that followed. The report attributes both declines to how UDISE+ data itself is used, allowing planners to reallocate teachers to where enrolment actually needs them, rather than leaving schools overstaffed relative to the students they serve.School infrastructure has improved along with the workforce. Computer access rose from 47.7% in 2022-23 to 69.9% in 2025-26, with the sharpest single-year jump, a 9.5 percentage point rise, coming in 2023-24. Internet access followed a close path, up from 49.7% to 67.4% over the same period. Basic facilities are now close to universal: 95.0% of schools have electricity, up from 91.7%; 99.5% have drinking water; 98.5% have girls' toilets and 97.2% have boys' toilets; and 96.9% have handwashing facilities, up from 94.1% four years ago. Library access has also grown steadily, from 88.3% to 90.5% of schools. Two areas lag behind the rest — playgrounds, present in 81.9% of schools, actually declined slightly from 83.0% the previous year, breaking an otherwise uninterrupted rise since 2022-23, and rainwater harvesting remains available in just 29.9% of schools despite steady incremental gains each year since a base of 28.0% in 2022-23. Ramps and handrails for students with disabilities have grown from 51.0% to 58.2% of schools, though more than four in ten schools still lack them.The report also points to a shift in who is doing the teaching. Women now make up 54.9% of India's teachers, up from 52.3% four years ago and 53.3% the year after that — a steady climb of more than two-and-a-half percentage points across a workforce of over a crore people.Girls' enrolment has moved more slowly but just as consistently, from 48.0% in 2022-23 to 48.1%, then 48.3%, and now 48.4% in 2025-26 — small annual shifts that add up to real change in a system enrolling tens of millions of students each year.Read together, the UDISE+ 2025-26 numbers show a system that added capacity, tightened ratios and expanded infrastructure over four years, while still carrying a few gaps that didn't move like the rest of the data — a middle-school dropout rate that rose instead of fell, a Foundational and Preparatory retention dip after years of improvement, a zero-enrolment number that spiked before it fell, and a playground shortfall the other infrastructure numbers don't quite explain. None of these gaps undoes the larger trend, but they're the parts of the report worth watching in the years ahead, since they mark the points where the steady four-year climb didn't hold.
Article Summary: India's teacher count rose from 94,83,294 in 2022-23 to 98,07,600 in 2023-24, then to 1,01,22,420 in 2024-25 and 1,02,73,020 in 2025-26. The numbers show a workforce that has grown steadily even as the system around it has become leaner and retained more students.

NEW DELHI: The Delhi high court has imposed costs of Rs 1 lakh on the Delhi Transport Corporation (DTC) for pursuing a 32-year-old dispute with a bus conductor over payment of 17 months' back wages, terming the prolonged litigation an abuse of the process of law.According to PTI report, Justice Amit Mahajan dismissed the DTC's challenge to a 2004 Industrial Tribunal order in favour of the conductor, observing that the department's continued litigation over the limited claim had resulted in avoidable expenditure of public money.The court, in its September 2 order, said the DTC could recover the costs from the officer responsible for pursuing what it described as an "insignificant dispute". Of the Rs 1 lakh imposed, Rs 25,000 will be paid to the Delhi High Legal Services Committee, Rs 50,000 to the PM Relief Fund and Rs 25,000 to the conductor.The dispute dates back to November 1994, when the conductor was accused of failing to issue tickets to three passengers despite collecting a total fare of Rs 67. He was suspended following the incident.Although the enquiry officer had ruled in the conductor's favour, the disciplinary authority disagreed and issued a show-cause notice proposing his removal from service.He was subsequently removed with effect from August 1996.The conductor challenged the action, following which the DTC chairman-cum-managing director set aside his removal. In 1998, the DTC chairman ordered his reinstatement but denied him back wages and reduced his pay scale.The dispute then reached the Industrial Tribunal, which in 2004 held that the punishment was illegal and without basis. It ruled that the conductor was entitled to wages on his regular pay scale, along with arrears arising from the reduced wages and regular wages for the relevant period.The high court stayed the tribunal's order in July 2005, but Justice Mahajan found no legal ground to interfere with the tribunal's findings. The court noted that the DTC had failed to produce the enquiry report or establish a lawful basis for disagreeing with the enquiry officer.Justice Mahajan said the tribunal had taken a "reasonable and plausible view" based on the material before it and that its findings were neither perverse nor legally unsustainable.The court also criticised the DTC for litigating the issue of 17 months' back wages for 32 years, saying the prolonged proceedings over such a limited claim amounted to an abuse of the process of law and caused unnecessary expenditure of public money.
Article Summary: The Delhi high court has imposed costs of Rs 1 lakh on the Delhi Transport Corporation (DTC) for pursuing a 32-year-old dispute with a bus conductor. Justice Amit Mahajan dismissed the DTC's challenge to a 2004 Industrial Tribunal order in favour of the conductor. Article Title: TOI Social Impact Summit: 'Tech could bridge edu divide if personalised, won’t replace teachers'
